As a European reading both the article and these rather emotional comments, I am slightly bemused. The United States has always championed free trade and national sovereignty. Surely Canada is therefore free to seek more reliable and more predictable markets—particularly amid Trump’s rather pointless tariff bonanza.

Yes, the EU is an administrative colossus and moves with the elegance and speed of an oil tanker. We Europeans know this better than anyone. Yet, its single market means  access to one of the world’s largest integrated economie (27 countries). 

Reducing barriers to goods, services and people is generally a good thing—or at least it used to be when Americans advocated it ;-)

So perhaps its advisable to take a breath. Canada is not betraying anyone. It is simply diversifying away from an increasingly erratic trading partner. That is not anti-American; it is rather basic risk management.

comments.name: chris bullard

The aggressive unraveling of U.S.-Canada trade relations and the imposition of crippling 50 percent tariffs represent a shameful, corrupt attempt to subjugate Canada into a modern vassal state.

The recent negotiations were never about mutual prosperity; they were a thinly veiled power play orchestrated to dismantle Canadian economic autonomy and force total alignment with U.S. interests.

Through erratic ultimatums and bad-faith maneuvering, Washington has made it clear that it expects Canada to accept the status of an economic dependent rather than an equal sovereign.

The corruption of this process is evident in how domestic political grievances and sectoral industry lobbies hijacked a near-complete agreement.

Pushing last-minute restrictions on Canadian manufacturing, attempting to muzzle independent foreign policy, and demanding the rollback of cultural protections expose a predatory agenda.

True trade partnerships rely on trust and reciprocity, but the Trump administration's tactics rely on intimidation, economic warfare, and open threats regarding national viability.

As Canada stands firm against these punitive measures and prepares counter tariffs, the mask has slipped entirely. What Washington demands is not a trade deal, but submission.

This blatant effort to dominate a neighbor exposes a profound moral and political bankruptcy in contemporary U.S. trade diplomacy.

Trump's a hot mess, dump him in the mid-terms, impeach and remove.

My first job in “The Film Business” was working in the film laboratory at Wilding Films (Charlie Chaplin’s original movie studio) in Chicago. My first job there was in the lab, working with the color timers, who were the “color correctors” for the final 35mm print shipped to the network/studio/theater.  A color timer would look at the film negative unprojected and choose different tints to filter the light as it was being projected onto unexposed film as a “copy” of the original negative.  My job was to create a notch in the edge of the 35mm film so the different “tints” would be triggered as the print negative was exposed from the original negative.   Today, this procedure would be done digitally in basic Photoshop. This was my job for a yearly salary of $6,700 in 1966.
Over three years at Wilding, I moved up to working with the film editors who creatively shaped the story of the commercial or feature film.   It’s where I discovered that the editor is the most creative part of filmmaking.  He can tell many different stories, depending on the producers' input.

I've found that even colleagues who just use AI individually for work (usually LLMs in my field) seem increasingly incapable of recognizing the low level of quality it often produces.

They might feel like it generates stuff instantaneously that on the surface level looks professional, but there are often fundamental flaws or really stilted inauthentic/unclear language obviously generated by ChatGPT, etc. They wind up passing on the burden of having to untangle weirdly parsed language or unclear statements onto other colleagues, *or* just wind up with an increasing amount of materials that are 1 step away from AI slop.

It's also become increasingly hard to point out these issues, because the users often seem to take it personally and/or frame it into some greater ideological conflict, instead of just figuring out how to maintain high-quality & authentic material/content and communications. I think a big part of that is a result of the way ChatGPT, Claude, etc, are programmed to interact with users - creating the illusion of a collaborator where everything the user says & does is correct, and really pushing a lot of carefully calibrated psychological buttons that pulls them in on a personal level.

I am definitely not an AI luddite and think it's fascinating tech. But from my experience I think the issues I'm describing are becoming epidemic in workplaces, and causing more friction & quality decline than is commonly reported.

comments.body: Nice to see a fine craftsman get a researched obit here, with relevant photos.  Most minor, tiny note:  hide glue, really universal in the traditional violin world, does not dry; it just sets as it cools. (Photo caption).  This makes it easily parted for repairs, which, on good violins, are expected over the years.  I’m surprised at the number of independent violin luthiers being only about one hundred in the US.  Perhaps only ones who can  make a living solely by custom building.  The craft,  using  hand tools and ancient techniques, is alive and well, both for violins and many other instruments.  Modern technology has enabled luthiers, especially, to understand how to make better instruments for specific purposes, while still allowing for traditional methods used by one-person shops.

I'm struggling to understand how a 34th Street busway doesn't simply shift traffic onto the surrounding residential streets.

People still need cars. Seniors, people with disabilities, families, and countless others rely on being picked up and dropped off at their door. And unless the Lincoln and Midtown Tunnels are closing during busway hours, that traffic isn't disappearing. It has to go somewhere.

I support public transit and congestion pricing, and I understand why many people see the 14th Street busway as a success. But 34th Street is different. It connects access into and out of the city - 14th Street does not. 

What I'm looking for is a real plan for the people who live here. If traffic is being diverted, where is it going, and how will the city ensure that the surrounding neighborhood remains safe and livable for residents?

Despite my aversion to any kind of glorifying warfare I went to see this and was enthralled.  Seeing what it must have been like to be in a tight cluster of soldiers, facing the enemy cluster a few yards away, both sides with muskets that have poor aim and need manual reloading… omg. 

I was impressed that while the royal army and the Hessians were outfitted in smart-looking uniforms, true to form, the continental soldiers were more of a rag-tag crew with worn britches and unwashed jackets. 

Okay, so there was none of the misery of the gruesome blood and gore, but there was a nod to the “fallen” and wounded as an occasional soldier was killed or escorted off to be tended. 

If the pacing was accurate, I got the feeling that these battles were as ponderous as a slow baseball game. Incredible.

This hurricane story should be revisited in December.  Asking “Where are all the hurricanes?” today is premature.

The more interesting aspect of this issue is the very serious prediction made by NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) in May of this year. 

Start with this: An average season has 14 named storms, seven of which are hurricanes, including three major hurricanes. NOAA predicted 8 to 14 named storms, 3 to 6 hurricanes, and 1 to 3 major hurricanes. Stated differently, NOAA predicted a 35 percent change of a near-normal season, a 10-percent chance of an above-normal season, and a 55-percent chance of a below-normal season.  

https://www.wfsb.com/2026/05/21/noaa-reveals-predictions-2026-atlantic-hurricane-season/

NOAA didn’t make a mid-September Atlantic hurricane prediction, it made a hurricane season prediction.

Let’s wait and see.

Opera requires an extended attention span, something that an increasing number of people today lack (in our era of mindless social media and endless distraction).  It also requires an appreciation for history, of both the time and place within which a work was written, and the era that it seeks to portray.  And given the vast number of performers involved, and costs that their engagement entails, it probably also requires state support (as it routinely receives in Europe) to endure into the 2nd half of the 21st century.

That said, no matter what happens with the opera house, it will live on for its enthusiasts (like me) so long as recordings and videos continue to exist.  That’s the hopeful news.

comments.name: Tim
comments.body: "Look at this great historical figure from the past who perfectly aligns with the book I just wrote."   Mr. Sachs is a wonderful author who is also 80 years old and looking through the lens of the past. Invoking the ghost of Toscanini to solve modern structural problems is one way to look at the state of 0pera, but respectfully I suggest there are other ways more appropriate.  The Met may be hurting financially, but it's staging incredible operas - exhibit A being last season's staging of Saariaho's Innocence. Lyric Opera is absolutely causing a buzz in Chicago. Lyric has gotten younger people into the building - it's high energy now, and dare I say - trendy. Last season, after staging Mellon Collie and Infinite Sadness, Billy Corgan, founder of the Smashing Pumpkins, joined the Board of Directors. The times have changed, and opera needs to change as well. Subscriptions may be down, but that doesn't mean Opera is in trouble; it just means opera companies need to get creative in filling the seats. I'm not rejecting Mr. Sachs's opinion at all, I'm just saying the "fix" is not binary. I'll be in the Lyric Opera House for Don Giovanni next month and look forward to the future of opera in Chicago.

comments.name: L Owen
comments.body: My late husband, the baritone Joseph Shore, and I discussed the diminishment of opera in real time often.  He was fired from the Met after winning the Met auditions for performing Rigoletto against their wishes at the age of 27. When I met him, I was AD-ing in Macbeth with Arizona Opera, under the leadership of Maestro James P. Sullivan.  We did four operas a year, performed in Tucson and Phoenix, and we spent a month on rehearsals, which everyone said was crazy but which Jim Sullivan said was necessary.  The young singers -- and current stars in their prime -- that I worked with were eager and singing in their fach, and they considered opera the pinnacle of dramatic works.  But.  Universities all over the US and Canada were churning out singers with MFA's in voice whose actual voices were tiny, whom could be barely heard on stage, and who were dismissive of the great tradition of bel canto singing.  My ex once said he had a voice student who came aboard in a doctoral program, a soprano, who had never listened to Maria Callas.  This lack of knowledge became normal.  If you looked good, you were promoted.  If you looked great on TV, you were promoted.  All the opera lovers I grew up with knew the stories and had read the libretti.  We didn't need the Ruth and Thomas Martin translation above the stage.  We knew the music told you everything.  But opera is not passive.  It's not flicking through Insta.  You work for your catharsis. When it comes, it's glorious.

comments.body:
Hi —

Erin, you said “newsrooms and media companies are major centers of power” which “deserve the same kind of scrutiny and accountability” as governments & corporations.

And Michael, you said “as journalists, it’s important for us to hold our peers to account; trust is our most precious currency.” You also said the NYT doesn’t go easier on NYT alumni.

Does the NYT go easier on current NYT journalists?

Also, the NYT says curiosity is one of its values — that “Open-minded inquiry is at the heart of our mission. In all our work, we believe in continually asking questions, seeking out different perspectives and searching for better ways of doing things.”

But I worked for the NYT & they ended my contract just for asking a reasonable, uncontroversial question the editor I asked was happy to answer. 

NYT media reporters aren’t scrutinizing that or even trying to verify it, as far as I know. Current NYT journalists are not being held to account for this hypocrisy. Why not?

How does the NYT getting rid of journalists for asking questions benefit journalism, democracy or the public?

It’s a hypocritical & dangerous abuse of power, & it’s gone unaddressed & been buried by the NYT. Why?

You say trust is crucial. But why should I trust editorial decisions as much as I did when I worked there when I’ve been treated unfairly & hypocritically by some of the same journalists who make those decisions?

comments.name: wrenhunter
comments.body:
Great conversation, and I really appreciate the insider perspective. This quote struck me:

"When I’m worried I may have a story wrong, my solution is usually five or 10 additional phone calls."

This is exactly what Woodward and Bernstein did in the film “All the President’s Men“. Of course, even then, they weren’t sure they got it right and they took a lot of flack.

So I find it odd that many people venerate them, but in the comments on many Times stories, you see bitter accusations of reporters leaving things out, not pressing hard enough, and general exhortations to “do better“.

I think in this era of partisanship and polarization, the measured approach taken by The Times is more important than ever, and I appreciate it.

By the way, I don’t work for the company, and I’m not even a reporter. Just an interested citizen.
